Counts recorded per region and per year carry two kinds of structure at once.
Neighbouring regions look alike, consecutive years look alike, and sometimes
the map itself changes over time: an outbreak that starts in one corner and
spreads, a decline that hits the north first. This article fits such data with
tulpa from the simplest model, a spatial field plus a time trend, up to the four
interaction types of Knorr-Held (2000).
It ends with maps per time slice, a forecast for two held-out years, a
comparison of the models, and a table of which door fits which model.
It builds on [Spatial models](spatial-models.html) and
[Temporal models](temporal-models.html), and the interaction blocks use the
`tgmrf()` construction from [Custom latent blocks](tgmrf.html).

Installation is covered in [Get started](tulpa.html). The interaction blocks
are sparse precision matrices built with Matrix.

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
library(Matrix)
```

## The model

Consider $S$ regions observed at $T$ time points. Index the regions by
$s = 1, \ldots, S$ and the time points by $t = 1, \ldots, T$, and let $y_{st}$
denote the count recorded in region $s$ at time $t$, with a covariate value
$x_{st}$. The counts are Poisson with log mean

$$
\eta_{st} \;=\; \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{st} + u_s + v_t + \delta_{st},
$$

where $u_s$ is the spatial effect of region $s$, $v_t$ the temporal effect of
time $t$, and $\delta_{st}$ the space-time interaction: the part of the log
mean that belongs to the pair $(s, t)$ and to neither main effect alone.
Without $\delta$ the model is additive, and the map has the same shape at every
time point, shifted up or down by $v_t$.

The spatial effect is an intrinsic conditional autoregressive (ICAR) field on
the adjacency graph of the regions. With $W$ the 0/1 adjacency matrix and $D$
the diagonal matrix of neighbour counts, its precision is
$\tau_s R_s$ with $R_s = D - W$. The temporal effect is a first-order random
walk with precision $\tau_t R_t$, where $R_t$ is the ICAR structure of a chain:
$R_t = D_1^\top D_1$ for the $(T - 1) \times T$ first-difference matrix $D_1$.
Both structure matrices leave the constant vector unpenalised, and tulpa
removes that direction with a sum-to-zero constraint, so the intercept carries
the overall level.

The interaction is a vector of $S T$ values. Stack them region-fastest, so that
entry $(t - 1) S + s$ of $\delta$ is $\delta_{st}$. Each Knorr-Held type gives
$\delta$ a Gaussian prior with precision $\tau_\delta K$, where $K$ is a
Kronecker product ($\otimes$ denotes the Kronecker product, and $I_n$ the
$n \times n$ identity):

| Type | $K$ | What it says about $\delta$ |
|---|---|---|
| I | $I_T \otimes I_S$ | every cell independent |
| II | $R_t \otimes I_S$ | a random walk in time in each region, regions independent |
| III | $I_T \otimes R_s$ | an ICAR map at each time, time points independent |
| IV | $R_t \otimes R_s$ | smooth in space and in time |

The Kronecker form is what keeps the precision sparse. Entry
$((t-1)S + s, (t'-1)S + s')$ of $R_t \otimes R_s$ is $(R_t)_{tt'} (R_s)_{ss'}$,
so it is nonzero only when $t$ and $t'$ are equal or consecutive and $s$ and
$s'$ are equal or adjacent. A type IV cell is tied to its neighbours in space,
in time, and across both at once.

Types II, III and IV are intrinsic. The null space of $R_t \otimes I_S$ holds
every $\delta$ that is constant in time within each region, which is exactly
what $u_s$ already describes. The null space of $I_T \otimes R_s$ holds every
$\delta$ constant across regions at each time, which is what $v_t$ describes,
and the null space of $R_t \otimes R_s$ holds both. The interaction is
identified by removing those directions with linear constraints
$B \delta = 0$:

- types II and IV: $\sum_{t=1}^{T} \delta_{st} = 0$ for every region $s$;
- types III and IV: $\sum_{s=1}^{S} \delta_{st} = 0$ for every time $t$.

The rows of $B$ span the null space of $K$, so adding $\kappa B^\top B$ to the
precision penalises only the directions $\tau_\delta K$ leaves free. With
$\kappa = 1000$ the constrained directions carry a prior standard deviation of
at most 0.01 on the log scale for the sizes used here, and the determinant of
$\tau_\delta K + \kappa B^\top B$ depends on $\tau_\delta$ through
$\operatorname{rank}(K) \log \tau_\delta$ only, which is the normalisation of
the intrinsic density. This is how the blocks below are built.

## Simulating data

Put $S = 25$ regions on a 5 by 5 lattice, each adjacent to the regions sharing
an edge with it, and observe them at $T = 10$ time points.

```{r lattice}
nr <- 5; nc <- 5; S <- nr * nc; Tn <- 10
xy <- expand.grid(col = 1:nc, row = 1:nr)
W  <- 1 * (as.matrix(dist(xy, method = "manhattan")) == 1)
```

The spatial truth `u_true` is a gradient rising from the south-west to the
north-east corner, the temporal truth `v_true` one sine wave over the ten time
points. The interaction is a hotspot in the south-west corner that grows
linearly over time, centred over regions and over time points so that it
satisfies both sets of constraints and carries nothing the main effects could
take. On the log scale the three components have standard deviations of about
0.6, 0.5 and 0.1.

```{r truth}
u_true <- 0.6 * as.numeric(scale(xy$col + 0.5 * xy$row))
v_true <- 0.5 * as.numeric(scale(sin(2 * pi * (1:Tn) / Tn)))
g <- exp(-((xy$col - 1.5)^2 + (xy$row - 1.5)^2) / 2)
bump <- 1.2 * outer(g, (1:Tn - 1) / (Tn - 1))
delta_true <- bump - outer(rowMeans(bump), rep(1, Tn)) -
  outer(rep(1, S), colMeans(bump)) + mean(bump)
round(c(range = range(delta_true), sd = sd(c(delta_true))), 3)
```

Each region-time cell gets one count with intercept 1.5 (a mean count of about
4.5) and slope 0.4 on a covariate drawn per cell. The data frame is ordered
region-fastest, so row `cell` is entry `cell` of the stacked interaction.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(11)
d <- expand.grid(region = 1:S, time = 1:Tn)
d$cell <- seq_len(nrow(d))
d$x <- rnorm(nrow(d))
eta <- 1.5 + 0.4 * d$x + u_true[d$region] + v_true[d$time] +
  delta_true[cbind(d$region, d$time)]
d$y <- rpois(nrow(d), exp(eta))
head(d, 3)
```

`show_map()` draws one value per region on the lattice, south-west corner at
the bottom left, with the value printed in each cell. The true interaction at three time points shows the hotspot:
negative at time 1, positive by time 10, with the opposite sign in the far
corner that the centring puts there.

```{r truth-map, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 2.5, fig.alt = "Three lattice maps of the true space-time interaction at times 1, 5 and 10: the south-west corner turns from negative to positive over time"}
show_map <- function(z, main, zlim, pal = hcl.colors(30, "Blue-Red 3")) {
  image(1:nc, 1:nr, matrix(z, nc, nr), zlim = zlim, main = main, col = pal,
        xlab = "", ylab = "", axes = FALSE)
  text(xy$col, xy$row, sprintf("%.2f", z), cex = 0.6)
}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
for (tt in c(1, 5, 10)) show_map(delta_true[, tt], paste("time", tt), c(-0.4, 0.4))
par(op)
```

## Fitting the additive model

The additive model needs no new syntax. The spatial field goes in as in
[Spatial models](spatial-models.html), through `spatial =` and a
`spatial(region)` term, and the trend as in
[Temporal models](temporal-models.html), through `temporal =`. `ctl` keeps the
fits to two threads and switches off the progress lines.

```{r fit-additive}
ctl <- list(n_threads = 2, progress = FALSE)
fit_add <- tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region), data = d, family = "poisson",
                 spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
                 temporal = temporal_rw1("time"), mode = "auto",
                 control = ctl)
summary(fit_add)
```

`mode = "auto"` routed the pair to the joint nested-Laplace backend, which
integrates over a grid of the two precisions, `b1.tau` for the spatial block and
`b2.tau` for the temporal one. The slope interval brackets the true 0.4. The
intercept has a standard error of 0.033.

The two fields are read back with their own accessors. `field_effects()`
returns the spatial field per region; on this fit it reports the grid-weighted
mode only (`source = "mode"`, `sd` missing). `temporal()` returns the trend
with its posterior spread, from 2000 draws of the grid mixture.

```{r effects}
fe <- field_effects(fit_add)
head(fe, 3)
tp <- as.data.frame(temporal(fit_add, summary = TRUE))
round(c(cor_u = cor(fe$estimate, u_true), cor_v = cor(tp$mean, v_true)), 3)
sum(v_true >= tp$q2.5 & v_true <= tp$q97.5)
```

Plotted against the truth, the trend follows the sine wave and its 95% band
covers 9 of the 10 simulated values.

```{r effects-plot, fig.alt = "Estimated temporal effect over ten time points with a 95 percent band, against the true sine-wave trend"}
plot(1:Tn, tp$mean, type = "n", ylim = range(tp$q2.5, tp$q97.5, v_true),
     xlab = "time", ylab = "temporal effect")
polygon(c(1:Tn, Tn:1), c(tp$q2.5, rev(tp$q97.5)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.25), border = NA)
lines(1:Tn, tp$mean, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
points(1:Tn, v_true - mean(v_true), pch = 19)
legend("topright", c("estimate", "truth"), lty = c(1, NA), pch = c(NA, 19),
       col = c("steelblue", "black"), bty = "n")
```

### The direct fitter and an AR(1) trend

`fit_st_nested()` fits the same additive model from a response vector, a design
matrix and integer indices, without a formula. Its default temporal field is
an AR(1) process; with `temporal_type = "rw1"` it is the model above.

```{r st-nested}
fit_st <- fit_st_nested(d$y, cbind(1, d$x), d$region, W, d$time, Tn,
                        temporal_type = "rw1", family = "poisson",
                        control = list(n_threads = 2))
rbind(tulpa = coef(fit_add), fit_st_nested = coef(fit_st))
c(tulpa = logLik(fit_add), fit_st_nested = logLik(fit_st))
```

The two doors agree on the coefficients to the fourth decimal and on the log
evidence to 0.05. The AR(1) variant replaces the random walk by a stationary
process whose correlation `rho` is integrated on its own grid axis.

```{r st-ar1}
fit_ar1 <- fit_st_nested(d$y, cbind(1, d$x), d$region, W, d$time, Tn,
                         temporal_type = "ar1", family = "poisson",
                         control = list(n_threads = 2))
summary(fit_ar1)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "mean", "sd")]
c(rw1 = logLik(fit_st), ar1 = logLik(fit_ar1))
```

The AR(1) fit puts the correlation's posterior mean at 0.82 and its log
evidence 0.35 below the random walk's, so these data do not separate the two
temporal priors. `fit_st_nested()` also takes `spatial_type = "bym2"`,
`"car_proper"`, `"hsgp"` and `"nngp"`; the same pairs reach `tulpa()` through
`spatial = list(type = "bym2", ...)` or `spatial_gp()`.

### A continuous field with a trend

When the regions are points with coordinates, the spatial block can be a
nearest-neighbour Gaussian process (NNGP) on the coordinates instead of an
ICAR field on the adjacency. Here the lattice positions serve as coordinates.

```{r continuous}
d$lon <- xy$col[d$region]; d$lat <- xy$row[d$region]
fit_gp <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = d, family = "poisson",
                spatial = spatial_gp(~ lon + lat),
                temporal = temporal_rw1("time"), mode = "auto", control = ctl)
summary(fit_gp)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
```

The grid now runs over the field variance `b1.sigma2`, its range `b1.phi_gp`
and the trend precision `b2.tau`. With 25 locations the variance interval runs
from 0.16 to 4.85.

## Checking the additive fit

The additive model claims that every map is the same map shifted. A residual
check for that claim needs the in-sample linear predictor with both fields in
it. `predict()` holds an areal or temporal field at zero, so the predictor is
read from the grid instead: a nested fit stores, for every grid cell $k$ and
observation $i$, the inner Laplace mean `fitted_eta[k, i]` and variance
`fitted_eta_var[k, i]` of $\eta_i$. Mixing them with the grid weights $w_k$
gives the posterior mean and standard deviation of each $\eta_i$.

```{r eta-post}
eta_posterior <- function(fit) {
  k <- which(fit$weights > 0)
  w <- fit$weights[k] / sum(fit$weights[k])
  E <- fit$fitted_eta[k, , drop = FALSE]
  V <- fit$fitted_eta_var[k, , drop = FALSE]
  m <- colSums(w * E)
  data.frame(mean = m, sd = sqrt(colSums(w * (V + E^2)) - m^2))
}
ep_add <- eta_posterior(fit_add)
r_add  <- (d$y - exp(ep_add$mean)) / sqrt(exp(ep_add$mean))
```

`r_add` holds the Pearson residual of each region-time cell. A hotspot that the
additive model misses shows up as residuals that drift in the same direction
over time in neighbouring regions. The plot averages the residuals over the
five regions closest to the south-west corner and over the other twenty.

```{r residual-plot, fig.alt = "Mean Pearson residual of the additive fit over time, for the five south-west regions (rising from negative to positive) and for the other twenty regions (flat near zero)"}
sw <- g > 0.3
r_mat <- matrix(r_add, S, Tn)
plot(1:Tn, colMeans(r_mat[sw, ]), type = "b", pch = 19,
     ylim = range(colMeans(r_mat[sw, ]), -1, 1),
     xlab = "time", ylab = "mean Pearson residual")
lines(1:Tn, colMeans(r_mat[!sw, ]), type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
legend("topleft", c("south-west regions", "other regions"),
       pch = c(19, 1), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

The other regions stay within 0.2 of zero at every time point. The five
south-west regions swing between about -0.8 and +0.3 over the first six time
points and then climb, past +0.7 at time 9. A formal
version of the same check: fit a residual slope over time in each region, then
test whether neighbouring regions have similar slopes with Moran's I on the
lattice coordinates.

```{r residual-moran}
slope <- apply(r_mat, 1, function(r) coef(lm(r ~ seq_len(Tn)))[2])
moran_i(slope, as.matrix(xy), weights = "knn", k = 4)
```

Moran's I of the residual slopes is 0.21, against an expected value of -0.04
without spatial structure (p = 0.037), so neighbouring regions share their
residual trends. A dispersion test on the replicates the fit simulates checks
the count distribution as a whole.

```{r dispersion}
test_dispersion(fit_add, nsim = 100)
```

The dispersion ratio is 1.07 (p = 0.48). The counts show no excess spread
overall, and the interaction is found only by the check that follows regions
over time.

## Fitting the interactions

### Type I: an independent effect per cell

A type I interaction is one random intercept per region-time cell, so it goes
into the formula as `(1 | cell)`. On the nested-Laplace path its standard
deviation is integrated on a third grid axis, `b3.sigma`.

```{r type-I, warning = FALSE}
dI <- transform(d, cell = factor(cell))
fit_I <- tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region) + (1 | cell), data = dI,
               family = "poisson",
               spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
               temporal = temporal_rw1("time"), mode = "auto", control = ctl)
summary(fit_I)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
```

The outer grid now crosses 9 spatial, 9 temporal and 5 interaction nodes, 405
cells in all. tulpa warns when a multi-block grid takes more than 2 s to solve;
this fit and the interaction fits below sit near that limit on the machine that
built the article, and their warnings are not printed. The
posterior of $\sigma_\delta$ sits at 0.17 with an interval from 0.08
to 0.27, against an interaction whose true standard deviation is 0.107.
`ranef()` returns the 250 cell effects, here as grid-weighted modes without a
spread.

```{r type-I-ranef}
re_I <- ranef(fit_I)
head(re_I, 3)
```

### Types II, III and IV: Kronecker blocks

The structured types are built as `tgmrf()` blocks and enter the formula
through `latent()`. `st_block()` takes the structure matrix `K` and the
constraint matrix `B`, and returns a block whose precision is
$\tau_\delta K + 1000\, B^\top B$ with hyperparameter
$\theta = \log \tau_\delta$, a normal prior on $\theta$ and grid bounds.
`obs_idx` maps each row to its cell of the stacked interaction.

```{r kron}
R_s <- Matrix(diag(rowSums(W)) - W, sparse = TRUE)
R_t <- Matrix(crossprod(diff(diag(Tn))), sparse = TRUE)
one_s <- matrix(1, 1, S); one_t <- matrix(1, 1, Tn)
st_block <- function(K, B, name, idx = d$cell, mean = 3, sd = 1.5,
                     lower = 0, upper = 7) {
  C <- 1e3 * Matrix(crossprod(B), sparse = TRUE)
  tgmrf(
    Q = function(theta) as(as(exp(theta[1]) * K + C, "generalMatrix"),
                           "CsparseMatrix"),
    prior = function(theta) dnorm(theta[1], mean, sd, log = TRUE),
    init = c(log_tau = mean), bounds = list(lower = lower, upper = upper),
    obs_idx = idx, name = name)
}
```

The three blocks differ only in their structure and constraints, as in the
table of the model section. The constraint rows `kronecker(one_t, diag(S))` sum
each region over time, and `kronecker(diag(Tn), one_s)` sums each time over
regions.

```{r blocks}
B_II  <- kronecker(one_t, diag(S))
B_III <- kronecker(diag(Tn), one_s)
blk_II  <- st_block(kronecker(R_t, Diagonal(S)), B_II, "type II")
blk_III <- st_block(kronecker(Diagonal(Tn), R_s), B_III, "type III")
blk_IV  <- st_block(kronecker(R_t, R_s), rbind(B_II, B_III), "type IV")
blk_IV
```

The printed block confirms 250 latent values and a precision with 15.9% of its
entries nonzero. `fit_int()` adds a block to the additive model.

```{r fit-interactions, warning = FALSE}
fit_int <- function(blk) {
  tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region) + latent(blk), data = d, family = "poisson",
        spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
        temporal = temporal_rw1("time"), mode = "auto", control = ctl)
}
fit_II  <- fit_int(blk_II)
fit_III <- fit_int(blk_III)
fit_IV  <- fit_int(blk_IV)
summary(fit_IV)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
```

### Extracting the interaction

The interaction comes back from the outer grid. `tulpa_outer_grid()` returns
each cell's inner mode, with columns ordered as the blocks were stacked: the
fixed effects, the 25 spatial values, the 10 temporal values, then the 250
interaction values. Their grid-weighted average is the posterior mean.
`dc()` removes region and time means, which the type I estimate needs before it
can be compared with a centred truth; the constrained types satisfy it already.

```{r delta-extract}
delta_hat <- function(fit) {
  g <- tulpa_outer_grid(fit)
  cols <- g$n_fixed + S + Tn + seq_len(S * Tn)
  matrix(colSums(g$weights * g$modes)[cols], S, Tn)
}
dc <- function(M) M - outer(rowMeans(M), rep(1, Tn)) -
  outer(rep(1, S), colMeans(M)) + mean(M)
est <- list(I = dc(matrix(re_I$estimate, S, Tn)), II = delta_hat(fit_II),
            III = delta_hat(fit_III), IV = delta_hat(fit_IV))
sapply(est, function(M) round(c(cor = cor(c(M), c(delta_true)),
                                rmse = sqrt(mean((M - delta_true)^2))), 3))
```

Type IV recovers the hotspot best, with a correlation of 0.78 against the
truth, followed by types II and III. Type I, which shares no information
between cells, reaches 0.19. In the scatter the type IV estimates follow the
identity line and are shrunk toward zero at the largest true values, while the
type I estimates spread over the whole vertical range at every true value.

```{r delta-plot, fig.alt = "Estimated against true interaction for all 250 cells: type IV estimates follow the identity line, shrunk toward zero at the largest values; type I estimates scatter widely"}
plot(c(delta_true), c(est$IV), pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     ylim = range(est$IV, est$I), xlab = "true interaction",
     ylab = "estimated interaction")
points(c(delta_true), c(est$I), pch = 1, col = "grey40")
abline(0, 1)
legend("topleft", c("type IV", "type I"), pch = c(19, 1),
       col = c("steelblue", "grey40"), bty = "n")
```

## Maps per time slice

The quantity mapped is the space-time part of the log mean,
$\beta_0 + u_s + v_t + \delta_{st}$, read from the type IV fit as the
posterior mean of $\eta_{st}$ minus the covariate term at the posterior-mean
slope. The bottom row maps the posterior standard deviation of $\eta_{st}$.

```{r maps, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.6, fig.alt = "Six lattice maps from the type IV fit: posterior mean of the space-time log mean at times 1, 5 and 10 on top, its posterior standard deviation below"}
ep_IV   <- eta_posterior(fit_IV)
st_mean <- matrix(ep_IV$mean - coef(fit_IV)[["x"]] * d$x, S, Tn)
st_sd   <- matrix(ep_IV$sd, S, Tn)
seq_pal <- hcl.colors(30, "Peach", rev = TRUE)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
for (tt in c(1, 5, 10)) show_map(st_mean[, tt], paste("mean, time", tt),
                                 range(st_mean), seq_pal)
for (tt in c(1, 5, 10)) show_map(st_sd[, tt], paste("sd, time", tt),
                                 range(st_sd), seq_pal)
par(op)
round(range(st_sd), 3)
```

The means carry the south-west to north-east gradient at every time point and
the change of level with the trend. The standard deviations range from
`r round(min(st_sd), 2)` to `r round(max(st_sd), 2)`; they are largest where
the mean is lowest, since a cell with a small expected count carries less
information about its log mean.

## Forecasting two years ahead

A random walk extends past the data in closed form. Given $v_T$, the effect
$h$ steps ahead is $v_{T+h} = v_T + \epsilon$ with
$\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, h / \tau_t)$, and a type II interaction adds its
own walk in each region, with variance $h / \tau_\delta$. The forecast of
$\eta_{s, T+h}$ is the posterior of $\eta_{sT}$ plus these innovations, with
the covariate term moved to the new $x$.

To check the forecast against data, fit the additive and the type II models to
the first eight time points and hold out times 9 and 10.

```{r fit-past, warning = FALSE}
past <- d[d$time <= 8, ]
blk_past <- st_block(kronecker(crossprod(diff(diag(8))), Diagonal(S)),
                     kronecker(matrix(1, 1, 8), diag(S)), "type II",
                     idx = past$cell)
fp_add <- tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region), data = past, family = "poisson",
                spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
                temporal = temporal_rw1("time"), mode = "auto", control = ctl)
fp_II  <- tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region) + latent(blk_past), data = past,
                family = "poisson",
                spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
                temporal = temporal_rw1("time"), mode = "auto", control = ctl)
```

`forecast_st()` draws the hyperparameters with `tulpa_hyper_draws()`, which
records the grid cell of each draw, draws $\eta_{s8}$ from that same cell, adds
the innovations, and draws a Poisson count. The type II walk is extrapolated
without its sum-over-time constraint, so its innovation variance is the
unconstrained one. The result holds a 90% predictive interval per region and
held-out time.

```{r forecast}
forecast_st <- function(fit, h, n = 2000, interaction = FALSE) {
  hd <- tulpa_hyper_draws(fit, n = n)
  k  <- attr(hd, "cells")
  last <- which(past$time == 8)
  E <- fit$fitted_eta[k, last]; V <- fit$fitted_eta_var[k, last]
  out <- lapply(h, function(hh) {
    new <- d[d$time == 8 + hh, ]
    var_h <- hh / hd[, "b2.tau"]
    if (interaction) var_h <- var_h + hh / exp(hd[, "b3.log_tau"])
    eta <- E + sqrt(V) * rnorm(length(E)) + sqrt(var_h) * rnorm(length(E)) +
      coef(fit)[["x"]] * rep(new$x - past$x[last], each = n)
    yrep <- matrix(rpois(length(eta), exp(eta)), n)
    data.frame(region = new$region, time = 8 + hh, y = new$y,
               lo = apply(yrep, 2, quantile, 0.05),
               hi = apply(yrep, 2, quantile, 0.95))
  })
  do.call(rbind, out)
}
set.seed(3)
fc <- list(additive = forecast_st(fp_add, 1:2),
           type_II  = forecast_st(fp_II, 1:2, interaction = TRUE))
t(sapply(fc, function(f) c(covered = sum(f$y >= f$lo & f$y <= f$hi),
                           of = nrow(f), mean_width = mean(f$hi - f$lo))))
```

Both models cover 42 of the 50 held-out counts with their 90% intervals, and
the type II intervals are wider by the interaction's own innovation. The plot
shows the south-west corner region, where the hotspot grows, and the opposite
corner.

```{r forecast-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Observed counts over ten time points for region 1 and region 25, the type II in-sample mean for times 1 to 8, and 90 percent forecast intervals of both models at times 9 and 10"}
ep_past <- eta_posterior(fp_II)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (s in c(1, 25)) {
  ys <- d$y[d$region == s]
  f_a <- fc$additive[fc$additive$region == s, ]
  f_2 <- fc$type_II[fc$type_II$region == s, ]
  plot(1:Tn, ys, pch = 19, ylim = c(0, max(ys, f_2$hi, f_a$hi)),
       xlab = "time", ylab = "count", main = paste("region", s))
  lines(1:8, exp(ep_past$mean[past$region == s]), lwd = 2)
  arrows(9:10 - 0.1, f_a$lo, 9:10 - 0.1, f_a$hi, angle = 90, code = 3,
         length = 0.03, lty = 2)
  arrows(9:10 + 0.1, f_2$lo, 9:10 + 0.1, f_2$hi, angle = 90, code = 3,
         length = 0.03, col = "steelblue")
  abline(v = 8.5, col = "grey60")
}
par(op)
```

The dashed bars are the additive forecast, the blue bars the type II forecast.

## Comparing additive and interaction fits

WAIC reads the pointwise log-likelihood off each fit's linear predictor with
every field in it, so all five fits can be ranked on it.

```{r compare-waic}
compare_models(additive = fit_add, type_I = fit_I, type_II = fit_II,
               type_III = fit_III, type_IV = fit_IV, criterion = "waic")
```

Every interaction model ranks above the additive one, which sits 6.7 units of
expected log predictive density (`elpd`) below the best, at a standard error
of the difference of 2.9. Among the interaction types the differences are
between 1.5 and 3.8 units, each within about one and a half standard errors.
The ranking puts type I first even though type IV recovered the interaction
best: WAIC scores the fit to these 250 counts, and a free effect per cell can
fit them as well as a smooth one.

The log evidence is defined for the fits whose grid axes all carry a proper
hyperprior. It is reported for the additive and the type I fit; on the
`tgmrf()` fits `logLik()` returns `NA`.

```{r compare-loglik}
compare_models(additive = fit_add, type_I = fit_I, criterion = "loglik")
logLik(fit_IV)
```

## Prior sensitivity

The prior on $\log \tau_\delta$ sets how much interaction the model expects
before seeing the data. The default block uses $\mathcal{N}(3, 1.5^2)$. A
second block centres it at 6 with standard deviation 0.25, a prior that expects
an interaction with roughly a twentieth of the default's variance.

```{r prior-sens, warning = FALSE}
blk_tight <- st_block(kronecker(R_t, R_s), rbind(B_II, B_III), "type IV tight",
                      mean = 6, sd = 0.25)
fit_tight <- fit_int(blk_tight)
hp <- function(f) summary(f)$hyperparameters[3, c("mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
rbind(default = hp(fit_IV), tight = hp(fit_tight))
M_tight <- delta_hat(fit_tight)
round(c(cor_default = cor(c(est$IV), c(delta_true)),
        cor_tight = cor(c(M_tight), c(delta_true)),
        sd_default = sd(c(est$IV)), sd_tight = sd(c(M_tight)),
        sd_true = sd(c(delta_true))), 3)
```

The tight prior moves the posterior mean of $\log \tau_\delta$ from 3.6 to 5.3.
The estimated interaction keeps its shape, with a correlation with the truth of
0.84, but its standard deviation shrinks from 0.103 to 0.041 against a true
0.107: the hotspot is drawn at less than half its size. With one count per cell
the data inform $\tau_\delta$ only weakly, and the prior on it decides the
amplitude of the map's change over time.

The main effects are less sensitive. `fit_st_nested()` takes
`hyperprior = "flat"` in place of the default penalised-complexity priors on
the two precisions.

```{r prior-flat}
fit_flat <- fit_st_nested(d$y, cbind(1, d$x), d$region, W, d$time, Tn,
                          temporal_type = "rw1", family = "poisson",
                          hyperprior = "flat", control = list(n_threads = 2))
rbind(proper = summary(fit_st)$hyperparameters[1:2, c("mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")],
      flat = summary(fit_flat)$hyperparameters[1:2, c("mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")])
```

Both precisions move by less than a tenth of their interval width.

## Practical guidance

### Which door fits which model

| Model | Door | Hyperparameters |
|---|---|---|
| ICAR, BYM2 or proper CAR + RW1, RW2 or AR(1) | `tulpa(spatial =, temporal =)`, `fit_st_nested()` | integrated on the grid |
| NNGP + temporal field | `tulpa(spatial = spatial_gp(), temporal =)` | integrated |
| HSGP or NNGP + temporal field | `fit_st_nested(spatial_type = "hsgp" / "nngp")` | integrated |
| type I interaction | a random intercept per cell in the `tulpa()` formula | $\sigma_\delta$ integrated |
| type I interaction | `fit_st_nested(re_idx =, sigma_re =)` | $\sigma_\delta$ held at `sigma_re` |
| types II, III, IV | `tgmrf()` block in `latent()` | $\log \tau_\delta$ on the block's grid |
| panel trend (`group_var`) + spatial field | refused by `tulpa()` | |
| non-separable space-time GP | none | |

`spatiotemporal()` and `spatiotemporal_gp()` describe the interaction and
non-separable models but fit nothing; both stop with a message that names the
doors above.

```{r refuse, error = TRUE}
spatiotemporal(spatial_car(W, group_var = "region"), temporal_rw1("time"),
               type = "IV")
```

`spatiotemporal_effects()` summarises an interaction block that a model
package's own fitter attaches to its fit; the `tulpa()` fits above carry none,
which is why the interaction was read from `tulpa_outer_grid()`.

### Cost against regions and times

`time_fit()` simulates an additive data set on an `nside` by `nside` lattice
over `Tk` time points and times one fit, additive or with a type IV block. The
table reports the outer grid size, the nonzero count of the interaction
precision and the wall time, measured while this article was built (two
threads, Windows workstation).

```{r cost, warning = FALSE}
time_fit <- function(nside, Tk, type_IV = FALSE) {
  xy_k <- expand.grid(col = 1:nside, row = 1:nside); Sk <- nrow(xy_k)
  W_k <- 1 * (as.matrix(dist(xy_k, method = "manhattan")) == 1)
  dk <- expand.grid(region = 1:Sk, time = 1:Tk); dk$x <- rnorm(nrow(dk))
  dk$y <- rpois(nrow(dk), exp(1 + 0.4 * dk$x + 0.3 * sin(dk$region) +
                                0.3 * cos(dk$time)))
  f <- y ~ x + spatial(region); nnz <- NA
  if (type_IV) {
    Rs <- Matrix(diag(rowSums(W_k)) - W_k, sparse = TRUE)
    Rt <- Matrix(crossprod(diff(diag(Tk))), sparse = TRUE)
    B  <- rbind(kronecker(matrix(1, 1, Tk), diag(Sk)),
                kronecker(diag(Tk), matrix(1, 1, Sk)))
    bk <- st_block(kronecker(Rt, Rs), B, "type IV", idx = seq_len(nrow(dk)))
    nnz <- nnzero(bk$pattern); f <- y ~ x + spatial(region) + latent(bk)
  }
  el <- system.time(fk <- tulpa(f, data = dk, family = "poisson",
    spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W_k),
    temporal = temporal_rw1("time"), mode = "auto", control = ctl))
  c(regions = Sk, times = Tk, grid_cells = nrow(tulpa_outer_grid(fk)$nodes),
    nnz = nnz, seconds = round(el[["elapsed"]], 1))
}
set.seed(5)
cost <- rbind(time_fit(5, 10), time_fit(8, 10), time_fit(5, 20),
              time_fit(5, 10, TRUE), time_fit(8, 10, TRUE),
              time_fit(5, 20, TRUE))
cost
```

The additive fit stays under a second at every size. The type IV fit solves
405 to 504 grid cells, each over all $S T$ interaction values, and its time
follows the nonzero count more closely than the number of cells. The
constraint term $B^\top B$ is dense within each time point and within each
region, so the precision holds about $S^2 T + T^2 S$ nonzero entries: 640
cells on 64 regions carry 50752 of them and took `r round(cost[5, "seconds"])`
s, 500 cells on 20 time points carry 25040 and took
`r round(cost[6, "seconds"])` s.

### Rules of thumb

- Start additive and check the residuals over time by region, as in the
  residual plot and the Moran's I test on residual slopes. Add an interaction
  when the check shows structure; here the additive fit's residual slopes gave
  Moran's I with p = `r signif(moran_i(slope, as.matrix(xy), weights = "knn", k = 4)$p.value, 2)`.
- Choose the type by what the interaction should look like. Type II suits
  regions with their own trends, type III maps that change shape from one time
  point to the next, type IV a change that is smooth in both. On these data the
  smooth hotspot was recovered with correlation 0.78 by type IV and 0.19 by
  type I.
- Do not choose among types I to IV on WAIC alone at this data size. With 250
  counts the four interaction fits sat within 3.8 `elpd` units of each other,
  inside about one and a half standard errors.
- Report the prior on $\tau_\delta$ with any interaction map. With one count
  per cell and a mean count near 4.5, moving the prior centre from 3 to 6 on
  the log scale shrank the estimated interaction's standard deviation from
  0.10 to 0.04.
- Keep the additive model when the residual check over time finds nothing
  and the WAIC gain of an interaction is within its standard error. An
  interaction adds one value per region-time cell: here the type IV fit
  carried 250 of them for a WAIC gain of 5.2 over the additive model, and
  the type I estimate, which shares nothing between cells, correlated with the
  truth at only 0.19.
- Budget the interaction fit by $S^2 T + T^2 S$: 64 regions over 10 times took
  longer than 25 regions over 20 times in the cost table.
